title: How we build an RPG world with ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude — and keep a shared canon
author: NexTutor
selftext:
Creator disclosure: I’m Marek, building AnyVerse at Nex41. I also build NexTutor, hence this account’s name.



For The Stellar Corridor, we work across all four models: ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude. Each contributes ideas, challenges the material and helps catch errors. I make the final editorial and canon decisions.



Here’s what that process looks like, and how it has shaped a world people can both read and play.



A question before a map



The setting began with one question: what happens to a civilisation that depends on enormous infrastructure it doesn’t understand well enough to govern?



It became a science-fiction world set in 2387. Humanity has settled 47 systems connected by passages built roughly 1.2 million years ago by the First Ones.



We established a constraint early: the network has no will. It doesn’t choose heroes, reward people or deliver prophecies. It is ancient material infrastructure.



That gives us a concrete editorial check. If a proposed plot depends on the network deliberately sending someone a message, it conflicts with the foundation.



Four models in the writers’ room



We develop scenarios, stories and visual concepts through work with all four models. Each brings suggestions and criticism; their contributions can change the direction of the material.



Gemini, for example, acts as a voice in that writers’ room. It develops alternative story dossiers, locations, conflicts and ecologies; proposes creatures, flora and artefacts; and challenges character stakes and costs. It also helps identify when a new story risks repeating an earlier one.



We compare those contributions with Claude’s, Grok’s, ChatGPT’s and my own judgment. A model’s proposal is material to consider, rather than an automatic addition to canon.



Canon decisions, final editing, implementation and publication remain our responsibility. We also manage the production and selection of illustrations and audiobooks. This describes our creative workflow, separate from the AI Game Master used during gameplay.



Scenarios gave the world its structure



The first three scenarios put the player in the role of an assessor: someone who gathers evidence, examines telemetry, hears competing claims and makes recommendations they cannot enforce themselves.



The conflicts involved access to a shared node, a measurable phenomenon mistaken for a message, and a colony losing its economic purpose when a new route opens.



That established the setting’s recurring tensions: access, responsibility, evidence and who pays when infrastructure changes people’s lives.



Expansion had to preserve those foundations



We later developed the Deep Corridor: older routes, incomplete maps, independent habitats, salvage crews, private endpoints and ports where the Confederation is a visitor.



We developed distinct populations too, with another constraint: biology must not become a character class. A character still needs a profession, debts, interests and loyalties.



Having those constraints gives us something specific to challenge when reviewing new ideas across the models.



Stories test how far the world can grow



The Last Vector explored rescue and the personal cost of independence.



The Reliable took us into a dead service ring and damaged infrastructure where a wall might briefly stop behaving like a wall.



This introduced uncontrolled, local breaches that can let matter, energy, images or living things through. Nobody chooses when they happen or what is on the other side.



It opened room for science-fiction horror while preserving the original rule: the network still has no intention.



Ecology has to change the experience



For the bestiary, each creature received an environment, hunting behaviour, a limitation and a possible human response.



On the ice planet Kharos-9, creatures change how characters move, stay quiet, mislead a predator or attempt a rescue.



When reviewing a creature concept, the useful question is: what does this make someone do differently in a scene?



Culture became playable



We designed Vektra as a card game people play inside the setting, around wagers, debts and reputation. Then we built a playable version on the website.



It has a 56-card deck, bidding, card exchanges and its own combinations and visual language. Its fictional origins connect to the First Ones, but the cards don’t unlock their infrastructure or reveal their secrets.



A reader can encounter it in a story and then play it themselves. That connection helps give everyday culture a presence beyond background lore.



The world now includes scenarios, stories in Polish and English, audiobooks, characters, locations, a bestiary and Vektra. Our goal is for reading and playing to reveal different parts of the same place.



Working with four models gives us more alternatives and more opportunities to spot problems. It also leaves us with the editorial work of deciding what belongs together. We don’t treat agreement between models as proof that an idea is consistent.



For others using several models in creative development: how do you keep their contributions coherent as a setting grows?

This is unpaid testing; honest criticism is welcome. AnyVerse is already live, with free and paid subscriptions.
